summary:
Active risk and a defensive reserve (0:00–6:58): Alex and Leila Hormozi and adviser Sharan argue that building a business and investing its profits require different skills. Alex says he chased 100% returns and lost money; Leila discovered a supposedly passive investor employed 45 people. Their proposed barbell keeps entrepreneurial risk in the operating company and delegates investments while building a reserve that can support future business bets. Their mentioned 15–20% targets are personal goals, not guaranteed or risk-free returns.

Deal flow and investment screening (6:58–16:07): The speakers advocate examining many opportunities and assessing managers rather than assuming an asset class is inherently good. They claim private deals outperform public markets, but do not establish that this holds after fees, risk, selection bias and illiquidity. Sharan's four-part investment X-ray asks about capital preservation, tax efficiency, cash yield and growth; size each position for your own circumstances rather than copying theirs.

Tax planning and cash flow (16:07–28:35): They describe US-specific incentives, deferral and accounting choices, and claim that better advice improved their own results. Alex reports surprise additional tax bills of $12 million and $17 million; the group argues for separating tax strategy from return preparation and planning before year-end. Their examples are not universal rules: revenue recognition and tax treatment are constrained by law, and deferral is not forgiveness. Obtain independent advice in your own jurisdiction before acting.

Verdict and commercial offer (28:35–31:25): Their conclusion is to adopt a few suitable, documented frameworks rather than pursue exotic tax schemes that introduce excessive risk. They promote a wealth workshop aimed at established entrepreneurs and accredited investors; the pitch and their own reported outcomes should not be taken as independent evidence of likely returns.
why_valuable: Helps a business owner decide how to separate operating risk from surplus investments, screen opportunities and ask a qualified adviser about tax planning without assuming US rules or the speakers' returns apply locally.
key_takeaways: 3:09 — Alex says his 100% return ambitions led to losses; separate business risk from a defensively managed reserve rather than demand startup-like returns everywhere.
4:14 — Leila found a supposedly passive operation employed 45 people; delegated investing still involves active work and manager risk.
7:01 — Treat deal sourcing as a funnel and scrutinize the individual operator; their private-market outperformance claim is not independently established here.
12:49 — Use four questions on capital preservation, tax efficiency, cash yield and growth before committing; the scores are subjective, not a valuation.
15:17 — Set position sizes based on your own exposure and tax circumstances; the speakers say their sizing is not a prescription for others.
19:42 — Their claimed accounting and tax benefits are US-specific and subject to legal rules; tax deferral is not tax elimination, so consult a local professional.
25:51 — Distinguish a tax preparer from a tax strategist, and plan ahead rather than waiting until December; the closing workshop is a commercial offer.

chapters.title: The challenge after the exit
chapters.description: The Hormozis say earning money and protecting it are separate challenges, and describe losing millions on earlier investment attempts. They introduce Sharan as an adviser and attribute their later real-estate, deal-flow and tax-planning results to his help; those outcomes are their own claims.

chapters.title: Separate business risk from invested wealth
chapters.description: Sharan describes pre-made money decisions and an active–passive barbell, while Alex admits that chasing entrepreneurial returns on investment capital produced losses. Leila's visit to a family office with 45 staff showed her that someone must actively manage assets even when the owner delegates the work.

chapters.title: A reserve enables focused risk-taking
chapters.description: Leila argues that diverting attention to a second investing business can cost more than delegating to experienced managers. Alex says a protected nest egg made him more comfortable taking business risks, though the level and nature of risk remain individual decisions.

chapters.title: Build a deal funnel and consider liquidity
chapters.description: The group compares sourcing investments to qualifying customer leads: review many opportunities and assess the operator, rather than dismissing an entire investment category after one poor deal. They favor private deals and accept less liquidity, but their broad claims of superior returns are not independently substantiated and illiquid capital may be inaccessible when needed.

chapters.title: Avoid cash paralysis and impulsive deals
chapters.description: Leila recalls leaving $9 million in a checking account because she did not know what to do, while Alex describes writing checks without appreciating how much revenue had been needed to earn them. Sharan suggests testing whether an investment can serve multiple purposes, such as a return and a legitimately available tax benefit, rather than investing under pressure.

chapters.title: Four questions for every investment
chapters.description: Sharan proposes scoring preservation of capital, tax efficiency, cash yield and growth, using Apple, Bitcoin and real estate as illustrative examples. The score is a subjective questioning aid rather than proof of safety or a substitute for analyzing price, risk and current tax treatment.

chapters.title: Position size and personal circumstances
chapters.description: Alex admits that he once sized deals as a large fraction of available cash without a consistent method. Sharan says their real-estate allocation reflects their own profits and tax position, and urges investors to discuss sizing with an adviser rather than copying someone else's allocation.

chapters.title: Understand incentives and document decisions
chapters.description: The speakers frame tax codes as incentive systems and discuss US opportunity zones, exchanges and the Augusta rule as examples of strategies they believe can be useful. These are jurisdiction-specific claims with detailed eligibility and timing restrictions, so their examples require independent professional verification rather than automatic application.

chapters.title: Accounting timing and growth cash flow
chapters.description: Alex reports two unexpected additional tax bills of $12 million and $17 million and credits improved financial advice with changing their position. The group argues that permissible revenue and expense timing can defer tax and preserve cash during growth, but the actual accounting and tax rules determine what can be recognized and when.

chapters.title: Choose advisers and plan before year-end
chapters.description: Leila describes the stress of tax payments while a fast-growing business was expanding its cost base, and Sharan warns against exhausting cash on last-minute prepayments. They distinguish return preparation from proactive tax strategy and suggest business owners learn enough to assess their advisers' competence.

chapters.title: Simple strategies and the workshop pitch
chapters.description: The speakers say larger, lumpier cash flows make tax planning more consequential and argue for a few documented strategies instead of exotic, risky schemes. They close by advertising a wealth workshop for established entrepreneurs and accredited investors, noting that early-stage owners may not benefit from all of its material.

How I got here…

23 yrs old: Left my fancy consulting job to start a business (a gym).
24 yrs old: Opened 5 gym locations.
26 yrs old: Closed down 6th gym. Lost everything.

32 yrs old: Started making free content showing how we grow companies to make real business education accessible to everyone (and) to attract business owners to invest or scale their businesses.

36 yrs old: I did a $106M book launch selling 3.6M copies of my $100M Money Models book, in 72 hours, breaking the Guinness world record for the fastest selling non-fiction book of all time.

Today: Our portfolio now does $250M/yr between 10 companies. The largest doing $100M/yr the smallest doing $5M per year. Our ownership varies between 20% and 100% ownership of the companies. Many of them we invested in early and helped grow (which is how we make our money - not youtube videos).

You either get an epic outcome or an epic story. Both mean you win. 

Keep crushing. May your desires be greater than your obstacles. 

Never quit,

Alex

title: How To Steal Any Editing Style With AI (Properly)
description:
🚀 Final Phase (all 18 skills in 1 platform + the Reverse Engineer engine): https://www.skool.com/finalphaseai/about
Every AI editor I've given away came from reverse engineering edits I loved. Now I built the engine that does it for me: give it 1 to 3 reference videos, it measures the edit frame by frame and builds you your own AI editor skill in Claude Code 👇

🆓 All my editors + 18 free skills (free Skool): https://www.skool.com/nextphase-5790
Already in Final Phase? Open the platform and go to Reverse Engineer.
Weekly calls in the Skool if you get stuck installing anything.

🔍 What "reverse engineering an edit" means
Every edit is a bunch of decisions: how long each shot lasts, when it cuts and what kind of cut, when it zooms, the colours, how many caption words at a time and where they sit, which sounds hit on the cuts, where the music drops. Measure all of that and you can rebuild the edit without ever touching their footage.

⚙️ The 7 steps
1. Links: 1 to 3 reference videos (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube or a file) + a name for your new style.
2. Measure: every frame, every cut and its type (new shot, jump cut, punch-in and how far it zooms), shot lengths, flashes, fades, black screens, colours, captions. The voice gets split from the music and effects, so it knows where the music drops, where the clicks, whooshes and booms are, and which cuts land on a word or a beat.
3. Look: sheets of every cut (2 frames before, 3 after), and Claude checks each one, because a flash can count as 2 cuts and a fast whip pan as 1.
4. Study: everything that makes the edit look the way it does, each claim measured or seen at a timestamp.
5. Build: your new editor, starting from the closest existing one (flash cuts → 1K Editor, colour chapters → Editor V3).
6. Test: it edits a raw recording of you in the new style, measures its own edit and grades it against the original, number by number, then fixes the biggest misses (up to 3 rounds).
7. Notes: you see the edit and the scorecard, and what you say becomes a rule in the editor, so it keeps getting better.

🧪 The test
Will Schafer's reel, the one behind Editor V3: 2 minutes, 2,901 frames, 83 cuts. It found the same things as the Editor V3 study: loudness -14.2 LUFS, the red, blue and teal backdrops, the cuts to black, the punch-ins and the booms. Then it graded one of my Editor V3 edits against the reel: 19 of 37 measurements matched. Pacing and sound match; the look (brightness, warmth, zooms) doesn't yet.

🛑 The rule
It learns the edit, not the content: never their footage, face, voice, music, logo or words. Only timing, pacing, structure, colours, text, transitions and how the sound behaves. Sounds it pulls from a reference are only a guide, and get swapped for free ones before a style is shared.

👥 Who it's for
• Creators: turn an edit you love (a vlog, a reaction channel) into your own editor, not a template.
• Businesses: a dentist sees a clinic's reel that performs and wants that look for their own videos.
• Agencies: a client sends a reel and says "make it like this". Build a style for every client.

💻 What you need
Claude Code (I use Opus 5.5 on my Max plan, so it's inside my plan). The measuring runs on your computer with free tools (FFmpeg, yt-dlp, whisper.cpp, Demucs, OpenCV). Works best on a Mac (Apple's built-in text and face reader). About 150 MB of study files for every 2-minute reel it studies.
Install: open Reverse Engineer in Final Phase → download the zip → copy the install prompt → paste it into Claude Code. Then fill in the "make a new style" prompt with a name and your links.

✏️ Correction
• 19 of 37: a re-run of the same scorecard later that day scored 20 of 37, which is what the platform page shows.

Reference reels shown for commentary: Will Schafer (@willtschafer), "The Life Cycle of a Creator pt. 2", and @vxwx8 on Instagram. Not affiliated with either. This video is not sponsored.
